spoken: Cross a pea plant that has round seeds with one that has wrinkled seeds, and every seed you get is round.
But grow those round seeds into plants, and wrinkled seeds come back, about one in four.
A friar counted thousands of them in a monastery garden, and found the first rules of genetics.
This is the story of Gregor Mendel's peas, and of numbers that some called too good to be true.
Mendel was a friar at Saint Thomas's Abbey in Brno, then called Brünn, in the Austrian Empire.
From 1856 to 1863, he used the abbey's garden to cross pea plants and follow their offspring.
Pea flowers fertilise themselves in the bud, so to cross two plants, Mendel opened a young bud and pulled out its stamens.
Then he dusted it with pollen from another plant.
He tested 34 varieties, kept 22 that bred true, and chose seven traits, each with two clear forms.
Seeds were round or wrinkled, and yellow or green. Seed coats were grey or white, with violet or white flowers.
Pods were inflated or pinched, green or yellow. Flowers grew along the stem or at its tip, and stems were tall or short.
Over those years, he grew and tested some 28,000 plants, most of them peas, and he counted their offspring.
Take seed shape. Mendel crossed plants with round seeds and plants with wrinkled ones.
The shape shows in the seed itself, and that same year, every seed was round.
Mendel called round dominant, and wrinkled, which had vanished, recessive.
The next year, he sowed them and let the plants fertilise themselves.
Wrinkled seeds were back in their pods, often beside round ones, with nothing in between.
From 253 hybrid plants, he counted 7,324 seeds. Of those, 5,474 were round and 1,850 were wrinkled.
That makes 2.96 round seeds for every wrinkled one, close to three to one.
He did the same for all seven traits, and each one landed near three to one, from 2.82 to 3.15.
All seven together gave 14,949 dominant to 5,010 recessive, which is 2.98 to one.
So why three to one? And how can a trait vanish for a generation, then come back unchanged?
Mendel's answer, in today's words, is that each plant carries two copies of a gene for seed shape, one from each parent.
Write the round version as a capital R, and the wrinkled one as a small r.
A hybrid gets a capital R from one parent and a small r from the other, and one capital R is enough to make a seed round.
That's dominance. The small r stays hidden, and it can be passed on.
Each pollen grain and each egg cell gets just one copy, so a hybrid's are half capital R and half small r.
Which pollen meets which egg, Mendel wrote, is a matter of chance.
He wrote the four equally likely meetings as fractions, the pollen over the egg cell.
Only small r over small r, one in four, makes a wrinkled seed.
Today this is drawn as a square, devised decades later by Reginald Punnett.
It predicts one pure round, two hybrids and one pure wrinkled, in every four.
So two round seeds in three should be hybrids, still hiding a small r. Mendel tested that.
Of 565 plants grown from round seeds, 372 made both kinds of seed, and 193 made only round ones.
That's 1.93 to one, close to the two to one he predicted.
Next, Mendel crossed plants that differed in two traits, round yellow seeds with wrinkled green ones.
The hybrids were all round and yellow. From 15 of them, he harvested 556 seeds, in four kinds.
There were 315 round yellow seeds, 101 wrinkled yellow, 108 round green, and 32 wrinkled green.
If the traits are inherited separately, three quarters of the seeds are round, and three quarters of those are yellow.
That makes nine sixteenths round and yellow, and the four kinds come in nine, three, three and one.
For 556 seeds, that predicts about 313 round yellow and 35 wrinkled green, with 104 of each mixed kind.
Seed shape and seed colour had sorted independently.
With three traits, he found 27 kinds of offspring. In the end, he bred all 128 true-breeding combinations of his seven traits.
Mendel presented all this to the Natural History Society of Brno, at two meetings in February and March 1865.
About forty people listened, and his paper appeared in the society's journal in 1866.
It wasn't unknown, but it was read as a paper on hybrids, and cited only about three times in 35 years.
Even Mendel seems to have thought his rules held only for some kinds of plants.
His hawkweed crosses didn't fit, since many hawkweeds, it turned out, make most of their seeds without fertilisation.
When Mendel became abbot, his duties largely ended his science. He died in 1884.
Then, in the spring of 1900, three plant scientists in three countries published within about two months, and pointed back to Mendel.
They were Hugo de Vries in the Netherlands, Carl Correns in Germany, and Erich von Chermak in Austria.
Historians now doubt that Chermak understood Mendel's laws, and how much de Vries owed to Mendel is still debated.
In England, William Bateson, nicknamed Mendel's bulldog, championed it and named the new science genetics.
Three to one is an average. Plant by plant, Mendel's counts wandered.
His first ten plants for seed shape gave 45 to 12, then 27 to 8, then 24 to 7.
One gave 19 to 10, under two to one, and another, he noted, gave 43 to 2.
Small counts swing widely, because chance decides which pollen meets which egg.
Let's have chance do the same. For every seed, we pick capital R or small r for the pollen, and again for the egg.
Here are ten imaginary plants, with the same numbers of seeds as Mendel's first ten.
They scatter just like his, from 21 to 11 on one plant to 29 to 5 on another.
Now keep going, seed after seed.
After 40 seeds, the ratio stands at 7 to one. After 400, it has fallen to 3.30 to one.
By 7,324 seeds, as many as Mendel counted, it has settled at 3.10 to one.
In Mendel's words, the larger their number is, the more mere chance effects are eliminated.
In 1936, the statistician Ronald Fisher tested how well Mendel's numbers fit.
Real counts miss a prediction by chance. Mendel's, Fisher argued, missed by too little.
Against 1,000 gardens run by chance alone, only 50 come as close to three to one as Mendel's seven totals.
That's about one garden in twenty. Lucky, but not shocking.
Fisher's point was that the luck kept repeating.
His sharpest point was a test in which Mendel grew ten offspring of each plant.
Sometimes all ten offspring of a hybrid look dominant, so Mendel should have found about 1.7 hybrids per pure plant, not 2.
He reported 399 hybrids to 201 pure, almost exactly two to one.
Fisher concluded that most of the data had been falsified, perhaps by an assistant who knew too well what was expected.
Daniel Hartl and Daniel Fairbanks replied that Mendel probably grew more than ten, and that the fraud charge could be put to rest.
Their 2008 book with others, called Ending the Mendel Fisher Controversy, found no reason to think he made up results.
Yet one of its authors, A W F Edwards, still found too little scatter in 84 of Mendel's ratios.
One can applaud the lucky gambler, he wrote, but when he is lucky again tomorrow, and the next day, and the following day,
one is entitled to become a little suspicious.
A 2019 reanalysis, adding the extreme plants Mendel himself reported, found about as much scatter as chance predicts.
Mendel also said he left out some small experiments that strayed.
The open question is how he chose, counted and reported his peas, not whether he grew them.
Mendel never knew what his factors were made of. For the wrinkled seed, the answer came in 1990.
Wrinkled seeds lack one form of an enzyme that builds starch, called starch-branching enzyme one.
In wrinkled peas, its gene is interrupted by an extra stretch of DNA, about 800 letters long.
The intruder resembles a jumping gene known from maize.
Without the enzyme, the young seed makes less starch and keeps more sugar, which draws in extra water.
Then, as the ripe seed dries out, it ends up wrinkled.
One working copy of the gene makes the enzyme, so the seed stays round. That's dominance, in chemistry.
It was the first of Mendel's seven genes to be found, and by 2025, all seven had been identified.
So here is what the peas were saying. Every plant carries two copies of each gene, one from each parent.
Each pollen grain and each egg cell gets one of them, by chance.
A recessive copy can hide for a generation, and shows again when two hidden copies meet, one time in four.
None of this shows in a single pod. It appears only when someone counts thousands.
Mendel's counts waited 34 years to be understood, and then they became the first rules of genetics.
All from a friar, a garden, and a careful count of peas.
